title: Greedy and backtracking in Java (List copies, remove overloads, bitmasks)
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Java code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Jump game, subsets, combination sum and word search with ArrayList backtracking, the remove(int) trap, boolean[] used and bitmask enumeration.
source: Oracle Java docs (List.remove, Arrays.sort, Integer.bitCount); CLRS ch. 16; LeetCode Jump Game, Subsets, Combination Sum, Word Search

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `boolean canJump(int[] nums)`. You start at index 0 and `nums[i]` is the maximum jump length from index i. Return true if the last index is reachable, in O(n) time using a greedy farthest-reach variable.
questions.explanation: Greedy works because reachable indices form a prefix: if you can reach index r, you can reach everything before it. A backwards "goal post" loop is an equally valid O(n) solution (it would need these checks adapted). For `[2,3,1,1,4]` the result is true and for `[3,2,1,0,4]` it is false.

checks.label: tracks the farthest reachable index with Math.max
uses i + nums[i] as the candidate reach
returns false when the current index is beyond the reach

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] nums)` that returns all subsets (the power set) of an array of distinct integers using backtracking. You may add a private helper method.
questions.explanation: The copy is essential: adding `cur` itself would leave every entry pointing at the same, finally empty list. There are 2^n results, each copied in O(n), so O(n * 2^n) time. An include/exclude binary recursion or a bitmask loop over 0..2^n-1 are also valid.

checks.label: adds a copy of the current path to the result
chooses with add and un-chooses with remove (backtrack)

questions.prompt:
A Java loop

```java
for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << 5); mask++)
```

 enumerates all subsets of 5 items. How many iterations does it run?
questions.explanation: `1 << 5` = 32 = 2^5, one iteration per subset. Bit j of `mask` says whether item j is included, so the loop needs no recursion.

questions.prompt: Among the 16 masks 0..15 that represent subsets of 4 items, how many satisfy `Integer.bitCount(mask) == 2`?
questions.explanation: These are the subsets of size 2, so C(4, 2) = 6: masks 3, 5, 6, 9, 10 and 12. Filtering masks by bitCount is a compact way to enumerate combinations for small n.

questions.prompt: Inside backtracking, `cur` is a `List<Integer>` and you just appended the `int` `x` at its end. Which undo step is always correct?
questions.explanation: `List.remove` has two overloads, `remove(int index)` and `remove(Object o)`. The index form on `size()` - 1 is both safe and O(1) for an ArrayList.

options.why: Correct: removing by index drops exactly the last element, even with duplicates.
The `int` overload removes the element at index `x`, which is the wrong element or an exception.

options.text: `cur.remove(Integer.valueOf(x))`, removing the first element equal to x
options.why: With an equal earlier element it removes the wrong one, corrupting the path.

options.text: `cur.clear()`, emptying the list after each recursive call
options.why: This destroys the whole path, so sibling branches start from nothing.

questions.prompt: In the Java subsets backtracking, why does the `for` loop start at `start` instead of `0`?
questions.explanation: Starting at `0` would generate permutations of subsets and duplicates. With `start`, the recursion tree has exactly 2^n nodes.

options.text: So each subset is built once, in index order.
options.why: Correct: moving only forward in the array yields every combination exactly once.

options.text: Because Java arrays must be read from the middle outward.
options.why: Arrays can be read in any order; this is not a language rule.

options.text: To avoid an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` on the first iteration.
options.why: The index `0` is valid for any non-empty array, so nothing would throw.
`add` accepts any element; there is no ordering requirement on indices.

questions.prompt: A backtracking method adds the path to the result and later calls `cur.remove(cur.size() - 1)`.
questions.explanation: Always snapshot with `new ArrayList<>(cur)` (or `List.copyOf`) before storing.
questions.assertion: Executing `res.add(cur)` instead of `res.add(new ArrayList<>(cur))` leaves every stored subset equal to the final state of `cur`.
questions.reason: `cur` is one mutable ArrayList that the recursion keeps modifying.

whys.a: Right: all entries are references to the same list, which ends up empty, and R is the reason.
whys.b: R is the explanation, not a side fact.

questions.prompt: Sorting activities in Java with `Arrays.sort(a, (x, y) -> Integer.compare(x[1], y[1]))`.
questions.explanation: Sorting by finish time is the first step of the earliest-finish greedy.
questions.assertion: This comparator orders the activities by finish time ascending.
questions.reason: `Integer.compare` avoids the overflow that `x[1] - y[1]` can cause.

whys.a: Overflow safety is a bonus; it does not explain why the order is ascending.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but the ascending order comes from the compare direction, not from overflow safety.

questions.prompt: Backtracking over subsets of n items recurses n levels deep.
questions.explanation: Depth n is tiny, but the number of results (2^n) is the real cost. Deep recursions such as DFS on 10^5 nodes can overflow the stack.
questions.assertion: The recursion depth of subset backtracking is only n.
questions.reason: Java allocates each recursive call frame on the heap, which is why deep recursion never fails.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true, but call frames live on the thread stack, which is limited, so R is false.

questions.prompt: Permutations use a `boolean[] used = new boolean[n]` array.
questions.explanation: Default values: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, null for references.
questions.assertion: A `new boolean[n]` array starts with every entry true.
questions.reason: Java initialises boolean array elements to false.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: R is true and is exactly why A is false; the array starts all false, meaning nothing is used yet.

questions.prompt: Match each backtracking need with the Java idiom that serves it.
questions.explanation: Each idiom serves one step of choose, explore, un-choose. clear() would wipe the whole path rather than the last choice.

questions.prompt: Complete the Java bitmask enumeration of subsets.
questions.explanation: The upper bound `1 << n` equals 2^n subsets. The `& 1` isolates bit j after shifting, and a non-zero result means that item is included.
questions.text: Loop mask from 0 while mask < {1}; item j belongs to the subset when ((mask >> j) & {2}) != {3}.
